summary: Registers the Enumservices 'web' and 'ft', using the http, https, and ftp URI schemes under the process defined in the ENUM specification, RFC 3761.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets a phone number point to a website or a file download site in the phone-number directory.

subtitle: Registers the ENUM service names 'web' and 'ft', so a phone number can point to a website or an FTP site.

tldr.problem: ENUM maps telephone numbers to services through DNS records, and each kind of service needs a registered name before a record can use it. Web pages and file retrieval had no such names.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the Enumservice 'web' with the subtypes 'http' and 'https', and the Enumservice 'ft' with the subtype 'ftp', following the process in RFC 3761.
tldr.outcome: A number's record can now say that a URI is a source of information (web) or a file-retrieval service (ft). The RFC was later updated by RFC 6118.

today: RFC 4002 is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 6118. The text here does not describe the changes, so read that RFC alongside this one.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ENUM (RFC 3761) turns an E.164 telephone number into a domain name and then uses DNS NAPTR records to look up which services are available for it. This document registers two Enumservices, 'web' and 'ft', as RFC 3761 requires for the services field of a NAPTR record.

Both services share one feature: the end points and their resources are primarily sources of information.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like adding two new labels to a phone book: 'website' and 'file download'.

sections.title: Enumservices as Hints
sections.content:
An Enumservice acts as a hint. It tells the client what kind of service the URI built from the record's regexp field is associated with. A single NAPTR record can carry more than one Enumservice, which means more than one service can be reached through the URI scheme. The registration MUST say what is expected when that record is used and which URI scheme results.

The services are NOT meant to fix the protocol or connection method. They describe the kind of interaction the end user expects, and the end system decides how to carry it out.

The same URI scheme can serve different services, and one service can use several schemes. So RFC 3761 allows a type and a subtype. Here the type names the service and the subtype names the URI scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: A label tells you what kind of thing is behind an address, but not exactly how your computer should go get it. The computer decides that.

sections.title: The Web Service
sections.content:
The 'web' Enumservice is registered twice, once for each URI scheme. With subtype http the scheme is http:. With subtype https the scheme is https:, and the resource can be contacted using TLS or the Secure Socket Layer protocol.

Both say the resource identified by the URI is capable of being a source of information. The RFC notes that the kind of information can be manifold. Contacting a resource by an http: URI usually provides a document, and that document can lead to audio, video or executable code. So one cannot be more specific about what to expect. Both registrations have Intended Usage COMMON and list no specific security issues beyond the general ones in the Security Considerations section.
sections.plainLanguage: The 'web' label says 'there is something to read or look at here'. It could be words, pictures or even a program, so the label does not promise more.

sections.title: The FT Service
sections.content:
The 'ft' Enumservice has the type ft, the subtype ftp and the URI scheme ftp:. It indicates a service usable in the manner specified for ftp: in RFC 1738, for instance file retrieval.

Like the web registrations, it has Intended Usage COMMON and no specific security issues beyond the general considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The 'ft' label means 'files can be fetched from here', like a shared shelf of downloads.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
ENUM uses DNS as a global, distributed database, so anything stored there is visible to anyone anonymously. The RFC compares this with a telephone directory, but warns that data can be harvested automatically and used to target spam, such as junk faxes or junk SMS. Because a person cannot easily get a spare phone number, a 'sacrificial' number is not possible. As a principle, the data subject MUST give explicit informed consent before data is published in ENUM. Removing data does not remove copies already taken, so any publication may be permanent.

For the services themselves, the user SHOULD be asked to confirm before a web page is opened or an ftp session started, and SHOULD be told whether the communication is secured. Evaluating a web page can run embedded or linked executable code, so the client MUST ask for confirmation and MUST NOT download and evaluate web content automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything in the phone book is public, and copies can never be fully taken back. So you must agree before your details go in, and your computer must ask before opening a link.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The IANA has registered the Enumservices 'web' and 'ft' using the registration process defined in the ENUM specification, RFC 3761. Each registration in the document lists the name, type, subtype, URI scheme, functional specification, security considerations, intended usage and authors.
sections.plainLanguage: The official keeper of lists wrote the two new labels into the official list.
